name: Head lice and nits: what the NHS says
summary: Head lice are tiny insects in the hair. The NHS says wet combing is tried first, then a medicated lotion or spray, and school is not missed.
keyPoints: The NHS says head lice are small insects up to 3mm long, and finding a live louse is the only sure sign.
The NHS describes wet combing with conditioner and a detection comb as the first treatment to try.
A medicated lotion or spray is the next step if combing has not worked, and a pharmacist can advise.
The NHS says children do not need to stay off school because of head lice.
The NHS lists repellents, electric combs and plant oils such as tea tree as unlikely to work.

body.heading: What are head lice and nits?
body.body:
Head lice are small insects that live in human hair. The NHS says they are up to 3mm long, which makes them hard to spot. Nits are the eggs that the lice lay, and they can be small brown or white specks in the hair.

Head lice are a common problem, but they are not a sign of poor hygiene. One NHS-affiliated leaflet says lice live in all types of hair, whether dirty or clean, short or long.

body.heading: What signs do head lice cause?
body.body:
The NHS lists small brown or white eggs in the hair and an itchy scalp as signs of head lice. Itching can have other causes, so it does not prove that lice are present.

Nits alone do not show that a person has an active infestation. The sources say the only certain sign is finding a live, moving louse.

body.heading: How do head lice spread?
body.body:
The sources describe head lice as spreading through close head-to-head contact. One NHS-affiliated leaflet says contact lasting around a minute is needed, and that lice can also pass on shared hats, towels or combs.

The search results also said most lice are passed between friends and family, not only at school. The NHS says there is nothing that can prevent head lice, but that regular combing helps to catch them early.

Because they spread easily, the NHS advises checking other family members' hair often.

body.heading: How can someone tell for sure?
body.body:
The NHS says the only way to be sure is to find live lice. This is done by combing the hair with a special fine-toothed comb, called a detection comb.

NHS inform notes that wet combing works better than dry combing, because hair conditioner stops the lice from moving. Lice that have been seen to move confirm an infestation.

body.heading: How does the NHS say head lice are treated?
body.body:
The NHS describes wet combing as the first method to try. Hair is washed with ordinary shampoo, covered in plenty of conditioner, and combed from the roots to the ends with a detection comb. Any conditioner will do.

Combing is repeated on a set pattern of days to catch newly hatched lice, with a final check that everyone's hair is clear on day 17. The NHS says short hair takes about 10 minutes to comb, and long, frizzy or curly hair can take 20 to 30 minutes.

If wet combing has not worked or is not suitable, the NHS says a medicated lotion or spray can be tried. Some of these need to be repeated after a week to kill newly hatched lice. The pack shows whether a product suits pregnant or breastfeeding women or young children.

The NHS says everyone in the household who has head lice should be treated on the same day. Family members with no lice or eggs do not need treatment. Lotions and sprays should only be used when lice have been found, not to prevent them, because they can irritate the scalp.

body.heading: What does the NHS say does not work, and do children stay off school?
body.body:
The NHS lists several products as unlikely to work. These include head lice repellents, electric combs for head lice, and plant oil treatments such as tea tree, eucalyptus and lavender oil. Herbal remedies are also on the list.

The NHS says children do not need to stay off school because of head lice. It also says laundry does not need a hot wash. A Welsh NHS leaflet adds that keeping a child out of school should not be used to manage head lice.

body.heading: When might a pharmacist or GP help?
body.body:
The NHS says head lice can be treated without seeing a GP. A pharmacist can advise on the best lotion or spray.

The NHS advises asking a pharmacist for advice if wet combing has been tried through day 17 and live lice are still present. If a lotion or spray does not work, the pharmacist can talk through other treatments.

In Wales, head lice treatment is covered by the Common Ailments Scheme at most pharmacies. Anyone worried about their own or a child's health can contact the GP surgery, or NHS 111 for urgent advice that is not an emergency.
